d_intro_1: There! A page of the Atlas blew in here. Its ink has gone pale.
d_intro_2: Pale ink needs light. But this room is kept dark.
d_intro_3: One thin beam comes in by the shutter. Let us turn the mirrors and send it to the page!
d_scholar_1: Welcome, small travellers. I am testing how light moves.
d_scholar_2: It runs straight until something turns it or stops it. Try my mirrors and see.
c_thanks: Thank you. We will try the mirrors.
d_scholar_dark_1: In a dark room, one thin beam is easy to follow. You can stop it with your hand, or measure it with a ruler.
d_scholar_dark_2: So the dark is not for hiding. It is for seeing better!
d_scholar_see_1: The museum's record says older books had sight leap out of the eye. He held the opposite: light comes from the thing to the eye.
d_scholar_see_2: So when I look at you, your light is visiting me.
d_scholar_see_2_f: So when I look at you, your light is visiting me.
d_scholar_bye: Test it yourselves. That is the best way to know.
d_scholar_after: A straight beam, turned five times. You did not take my word for it: you tried.

d_cat_3: She has found the warmest spot in the room.

note_1: Ibn al-Haytham was born in Basra around the year 965 and later lived in Cairo. His best-known book is on optics: light and sight.
note_2: The museum's record says he let light into a dark room through a small hole, to test that it travels in straight lines and that a solid body cuts it.
note_3: The same record says he held that light goes from the thing to the eye.
note_uncertain: Not from the records: this workshop, its cat and the mirrors on stands are invented for the game. The founder's pictures of this story show a glass prism; no museum record read for the scene says he used one, so the game does not show one.

ck_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Jazari described this clock in his book of machines, which one reference work dates to 1205. Every half hour figures move, a ball passes from the falcon to the dragon to a vessel with a gong, and the balls gathered tell the time.
ck_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game stands the parts in one row and has each set the next going. The record describes levers, chains and strings inside the elephant, and what was read for this game does not say how the falcon is made to let its ball go.
ck_note_4: The record does not call him the inventor of clocks or of robots. It says he improved display clocks and moving figures within an older tradition.

pro_1: In a quiet museum sleeps a great book, the Atlas of Stories. Every page holds the story of a person, a place or an invention.
pro_2: One night a storm blew the window open. Fifty pages flew out of the Atlas and scattered across ten worlds.
pro_3: Hudhud saw it all. Hudhud is a curious hoopoe with an orange crest who lives among the museum's shelves.
pro_4: In the morning Hudhud found you beside the empty Atlas. "I know the way," he said, "and you know how to ask. Let us bring the pages home together!"
pro_5: A page comes home when you understand its story: by a question, by a clever idea, or by a kindness. The Atlas and the storm are invented. The people and places behind the pages are real, or are stories marked as stories, and the museum keeps what it knows of them.

cf_count_1: The museum's record says al-Kindi wrote the earliest treatise on breaking ciphers that survives. In it he counts the letters of a long sample of the language, ranks them from most to fewest, and compares that with the symbols of the secret message.
cf_short_1: He warns that a short message can mislead. And he tests a guess by looking at which letters stand side by side and at the usual openings of messages.

ak_intro_1: The page of the Atlas is folded inside a box, and the box opens only for the right number!
ak_intro_2: Call the unknown a thing, then bring the problem to its simplest form.
ak_words_1: The museum's record says al-Khwarizmi wrote everything in words, not symbols: the unknown is a thing or a root, and the known amount is a number or dirhams.
ak_ops_1: His book is named after two operations: al-jabr, restoring, which removes what is taken away on one side by adding its like to both sides; and al-muqabala, balancing, which cancels like terms on both sides.
ak_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The locked box, the two trays, the three problems, the child who carries the box and every spoken line are invented for play.
ak_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Khwarizmi's book on al-jabr and al-muqabala brings every problem to one of six types, each with a rule and a proof by a figure. He wrote it for what people need in inheritances, trade and the measuring of land.
ak_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game's problems are of the simplest type, things equal to a number. The step of sharing among the things is the game's own. Nothing read for this game says he used trays or a pair of scales.
ak_note_4: The record says that solving equations is older than him, in Babylon, among the Greeks and in India, and that Ibn Khaldun names him as the first to write in this art.

id_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game has six, twelve or fifteen sheets, not seventy. Putting sheets in order by matching their edges is the game's own idea: nothing read for this game says how his maps were ordered.

jz_intro_1: The page of the Atlas is hidden among the animal cards, and the cards have lost their groups!
jz_intro_2: Do not judge by feathers or by wings alone. See what people call each one.
jz_divide_1: The museum's record says al-Jahiz divided animals in his book by how they move: those that walk, fly, swim or creep. He says that in this he follows the names known among the people of his language.
jz_birds_1: He notes that not everything that flies on two wings is a bird: locusts, bees and flies fly but are not called birds; the bat is counted among the birds though it has no feathers; and the ostrich has feathers but is not, for him, a bird.
jz_hoopoe_1: The record lists the hoopoe among the creatures in the third part of his book.
jz_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The cards, the trays, the girl who carries the cards and every spoken line are invented for play.
jz_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Jahiz divides animals into those that walk, fly, swim or creep, and among birds of prey he tells those armed with talons, like the eagle, from those armed with beaks, like vultures and crows. All eight creatures in the game are named in this passage of his book.
jz_note_3: This is al-Jahiz's division, more than a thousand years old, and it follows the names used by the people of his language. Science today sorts animals in another way: it counts the bat among the mammals and the ostrich among the birds.
jz_note_4: Made simpler for play: the game takes one passage of the Book of Animals. The record says the book is wider than its title, with language, customs and much other learning in it.

pp_intro_1: The page of the Atlas was soaked in the storm and torn. We need a new sheet!
pp_intro_2: Paper is made step by step, and each step has its place. But the cards of the steps are mixed up.
pp_story_1: The museum's record says an old report tells that Chinese craftsmen captured in a battle near the Talas river in 751 taught the people of Samarkand to make paper from worn-out rags. The record calls this a report handed down, not a proved beginning.
pp_how_1: The record gives the way it was made: rags of linen or hemp are cut small, cleaned and bleached, then pounded in water to a pulp and dressed with wheat starch, then lifted on a mould and shaken until the fibres hold together. The sheet is laid flat and dried on a wall, then rubbed and polished smooth.
pp_child_1: I hung the cards of the steps on a line to dry, and the wind blew them down. Now I cannot tell where each one goes!
pp_child_kind: It is all right. We will put them in order together.
pp_child_blunt: You should have pegged them to the line.
pp_child_kind_r: Thank you! Next time I will peg every card.
pp_child_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will peg every card.
pp_feather_1: A feather, caught in the mould! It is one of mine.
pp_feather_again: Nothing else is caught in the mould.
pp_done_1: The sheet is smooth, and the page of the Atlas is whole again!
pp_goal_curiosity_how: Ask both questions: about the old report and about how paper was made.

pp_goal_feather_how: Find the feather in the mould.

pp_note_2: From the museum's record: the Chinese invented paper. The part of the Islamic world was to receive the craft, adapt it and spread it. From Samarkand it moved to Baghdad, and on to Egypt, Damascus, the Maghrib, Jativa in Spain and other lands.
pp_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game makes each step one card in a row. For the pounding the record names mortars, stampers and paper-mills; the game shows one mallet.

ib_intro_1: The page of the Atlas has flown along a traveller's road. Let us follow his road, stop by stop!
ib_intro_2: A road is remembered by its order: where you set out, and then where next.
ib_left_1: The museum's record says Ibn Battuta left Tangier on Thursday the second of Rajab in the year 725 of the Hijra for the pilgrimage, alone, aged twenty-two.
ib_written_1: It says he did not write his journey down himself: Sultan Abu Inan ordered it written, Ibn Battuta dictated it, and Ibn Juzayy edited it.
ib_stage_story: He left Tangier and crossed North Africa, Egypt, Upper Egypt and Syria, then left Damascus for Mecca.
ib_stage_explorer: He went down the Red Sea to Yemen and Aden, then to Zayla, Mogadishu and the trading ports of East Africa, and came back by Oman and the Gulf.
ib_stage_challenge: He left Mecca and went through Iraq, Khuzistan, Fars and the Jibal, then to Tabriz, Baghdad, Samarra and Mosul, and then returned to Baghdad.
ib_child_1: My camel has lost its bell, and I cannot hear where the caravan has gone. I am afraid of being left behind!
ib_child_kind: Do not be afraid. We will follow the thread together.
ib_child_blunt: You should have kept closer to the caravan.
ib_child_kind_r: Thank you! I will hold the camel's rope tightly.
ib_child_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will keep closer.
ib_feather_1: A feather, caught in the saddlebag! It is one of mine.
ib_feather_again: Nothing else is caught in the saddlebag.
ib_done_1: The thread is complete. The page of the Atlas can land and rest.

ib_note_2: From the museum's record: the record sets Ibn Battuta's journeys out in eight stages, after an article in an encyclopaedia. The game follows three of them.
ib_note_3: The record says scholars do not take everything in the account as it stands: Ibn Battuta told of losing some of his travel notes and writing them again from memory, and the article holds that the editor of the account rearranged several of its routes. The order here is the order of the account as that article sets it out.

ts_intro_1: The page of the Atlas is going round with two circles in the observatory and will not settle. Bring it onto a straight line!
ts_intro_2: Two circles turn, and out of their turning a straight line can come. Try the speed and the direction.
ts_why_1: The museum's record says al-Tusi was troubled that Ptolemy's system departed from steady circular motion, so he devised a model of his own built from turning spheres.
ts_obs_1: It says the observatory at Maragha was founded by the Mongol ruler Hulagu at al-Tusi's suggestion, that al-Tusi oversaw its building and its instruments and was its first director, and that it had a large library and a school.
ts_girl_1: I clean these instruments every morning, but I do not know how to dust the small rings without bending them. I am afraid of spoiling them!
ts_girl_kind: Do not be afraid. Go slowly and hold each ring gently.
ts_girl_blunt: You should have asked someone to show you before you began.
ts_girl_kind_r: Thank you! I will turn each ring gently.
ts_girl_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will ask first.

ts_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The two circles on the page, the girl who cleans the instruments and every spoken line are invented for play.
ts_note_2: From the museum's record: al-Tusi's model of the planets' motion is called his most original achievement. It is a model of two spheres, the smaller turning twice as fast as the larger and the opposite way, so that a point on it moves along a straight line.
ts_note_3: Made simpler for play: the record speaks of spheres, and the game draws flat circles. What was read for this game does not give the sizes of the spheres. The game draws the smaller one half as wide as the larger, which is the size at which the arithmetic gives a straight line.
ts_note_4: The record also says the observatory at Maragha lasted only some fifty to sixty years, and that its learning was felt for centuries from China to Europe.

cq_objective: Cards about coffee have fallen out of the page of the Atlas. Put each card on the shelf where the museum's record treats it, then press Show the record.
cq_intro_1: Cards about coffee have fallen out of the page of the Atlas. Some are settled, some are tellings, and some are tales. How do we tell them apart?
cq_intro_2: We throw no card away. We put each one on its shelf: what the record states, what is told, and what is a tale.
cq_names_1: The museum's record says more than one name is credited with bringing coffee, and that so many names point to local traditions and not to one documented event.
cq_word_1: It says the coffee tree comes from Ethiopia, where it grew wild, and that tracing the name of the drink to the name Kaffa remains unproven.
cq_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The cards, the shelves, the keeper of the records, the child who tidies them and every spoken line are invented for play.
cq_note_2: From the museum's record: the drinking of coffee spread in Yemen from Sufi circles, because it helped them stay awake through nights of devotion, and from Yemen it passed to Mecca, Cairo and Istanbul.
cq_note_3: As for who brought it, the tellings differ: one credits the jurist al-Dhabhani at Aden, another al-Shadhili at Mocha. The record gives both and does not choose between them.
cq_note_4: Made simpler for play: there are only three shelves. The third shelf does not say the tale is a lie; it says the record's source does not take it as history.

ah_intro_1: The page of the Atlas has fallen into a dry fountain. If the water runs, the page will float up and out!
ah_intro_2: The water comes down from the mountain in the channel. Turn the pieces of the channels until the way is joined.
ah_water_1: The museum's record says work on the Alhambra began with an aqueduct from the mountains, so that water ran through the town and the palaces.
ah_court_1: It says the Court of the Lions is divided by two paths that cross, with a fountain at the crossing whose basin rests on stone lions.
ah_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The grid of channels, the dry fountain, the keeper of the water, the girl who sweeps the court and every spoken line are invented for play. The grid is not the plan of the Alhambra, nor of its waterworks.
ah_note_2: From the museum's record: work on the Alhambra began with an aqueduct from the mountains. In the Court of the Myrtles a very long pool bordered by myrtles fills the centre, and in the Court of the Lions a fountain stands where two paths cross, its basin resting on stone lions.
ah_note_3: The record says the stone lions probably belonged to an older palace.
ah_note_4: Made simpler for play: what was read for this game does not say how the water was led from the aqueduct to each court. The channel pieces that turn are the game's own.

kr_intro_1: The page of the Atlas was copied more than once, and the copies do not agree everywhere!
kr_intro_2: Compare copy with copy, sign by sign. A small slip shows itself to whoever takes their time.
kr_who_1: The museum's record says Karima al-Marwaziyya was a woman who transmitted hadith, lived as a neighbour of the sanctuary at Mecca, and transmitted the Sahih on the authority of al-Kushmihani.
kr_book_1: It says she kept her book carefully and checked it against other copies, and that leading scholars read hadith with her.
kr_boy_1: I carried the copies here as fast as I could, and now they do not agree. Did I spoil them?
kr_boy_kind: You spoiled nothing. Slips happen when a page is copied. We will find them together.
kr_boy_blunt: You should have checked them before you ran.
kr_boy_kind_r: Thank you! I will help you look, sign by sign.
kr_boy_blunt_r: I know. Next time I will check them first.
kr_feather_1: A feather, between two copies! It is one of mine.
kr_feather_again: Nothing else is between the copies.
kr_done_1: Every slip is found, and the page of the Atlas is free again!
kr_goal_curiosity_how: Ask both questions: who Karima was, and about her book.
kr_goal_ingenuity_how: Make no more than {n} wrong marks.
kr_goal_kindness_how: Answer the boy who carries the copies kindly.
kr_goal_feather_how: Find the feather between the copies.
kr_note_1: This is a game, not a history. The copies, the signs drawn in them, the boy who carries the copies and every spoken line are invented for play.
kr_note_2: From the museum's record: Karima al-Marwaziyya kept her book carefully and checked it against other copies. Leading scholars read hadith with her, among them al-Khatib. She died at Mecca in 463 of the Hijra.
kr_note_3: Made simpler for play: the game uses drawn signs in place of words, and shows nothing of the text of any hadith. Its rule, that what two copies agree on is right, is the game's own, and is not how scholars of hadith collated their books.
kr_review: Historical review pending: the museum record linked here has not yet been through historical review for this game.
jn_hub_note: The journey plays every page built so far, one after another. When a page is done, a door lights up: walk Hudhud to it to go on. Each page can still be chosen on its own below.
jn_panel_title: The page is home, and the door is open
jn_door_lit: The door is open! Let us go through it.
jn_objective_door: Walk Hudhud to the lit door at the end of the garden.
jn_alt_start: A corridor. Hudhud stands at one end; at the other end the door is lit.
jn_alt_along: Hudhud is walking along the corridor towards the lit door.
jn_alt_arrived: Hudhud has reached the lit door.

jn_end: Every page built so far is home. More pages are on their way.
jr_canvas_label: Al-Jazari's workshop, as a picture. The list after it says the same in words.
jr_objective: Fly to a part and touch it to pick it up, then touch a place on the clock to put it there. Pull the lever to set the clock going.
jr_objective_door: Walk Hudhud to the lit door at the end of the workshop.
jr_thing_box: the box on the high shelf
jr_thing_spare_1: the first spare part on the workbench
jr_thing_spare_2: the second spare part on the workbench
jr_spare_take: On the workbench: {part}. Pick it up
jr_lever_go: Pull the lever: set the clock going
jr_jazari_hello: Welcome to my workshop. Ask me what you like while you work.
jr_jazari_bye: Go well. The clock is waiting for you.
jr_note_room: The workshop, the workbench and the frame that holds the clock's parts are invented for play; they are not a picture of al-Jazari's clock.
jr_thanks: Thank you. We will try the clock.

tsr_objective: Touch the levers on the model's stand to set how the small circle turns, then turn the crank and see what path the point traces. Bring the page onto a straight line.
tsr_objective_door: Walk Hudhud to the lit door at the end of the observatory.
tsr_thing_girl: the girl who cleans the instruments
tsr_thing_shelf: the instruments on the high shelf
tsr_crank_btn: Turn the crank: turn the circles
tsr_last_none: No path has been drawn yet.
tsr_tusi_hello: Welcome to the observatory. Ask me what you like while the circles turn.
tsr_thanks: Thank you. We will try the circles.
tsr_tusi_bye: Go well. The circles are waiting for you.
tsr_note_room: The observatory, the model on its stand, the levers and the crank are invented for play; they are not a picture of the Maragha observatory or of its instruments.

akr_objective: Fly to the trays, the weights and the scoop and touch them to restore, balance and share. Bring the problem to one thing equal to a number, and the box opens.

akr_thing_box: the locked box on its plinth

akr_thing_less_number_left: the hollow coins on the left tray

akr_thing_less_number_right: the hollow coins on the right tray
akr_khwarizmi_hello: Welcome. Ask me what you like; the problem will wait on the trays.
akr_thanks: Thank you. Now to the trays.

akr_note_room: The room, the two trays on the table, the weights, the scoop and the locked box are invented for play; they are not a picture of where al-Khwarizmi worked.

kdr_objective: Fly to the signs on the shelf and carry each in your beak to a mark's place on the board. When every mark has a sign, ring the bell to read the page.

kdr_thing_page: the torn page on top of the bookcase
kdr_thing_slot: the place under {mark} on the board

kdr_kindi_hello: Welcome. Ask me what you like; the marks will wait on the board.
kdr_thanks: Thank you. Now to the board.
kdr_kindi_bye: Go well. The marks are waiting for their signs.
kdr_note_room: The room, the large board, the marks hung on it and the bell are invented for play; they are not a picture of where al-Kindi worked.
isr_canvas_label: Al-Idrisi's hall, as a picture. The list after it says the same in words.
isr_objective: Fly over the great table and touch a sheet to lift it, then touch another sheet to exchange the two. Exchange sheets until every seam matches.
isr_objective_challenge: Fly over the great table and touch a sheet to lift it, then touch another sheet to exchange the two. When you think every seam matches, touch the lamp to check the map.
isr_objective_door: Walk Hudhud to the lit door at the end of the hall.
isr_thing_stack: the stack of loose sheets on top of the tall shelf
isr_thing_sheet: row {r}, place {c} on the table, sheet {id}
isr_idrisi_hello: Welcome to the hall. Ask me what you like; the sheets will wait on the table.
isr_thanks: Thank you. Now to the table.
isr_idrisi_bye: Go well. Every edge has a neighbour that matches it.
isr_note_room: The hall, the great table, the sheets on it and the lamp are invented for play, and the drawing on the sheets is an imagined coast, not al-Idrisi's map.
rzr_canvas_label: Al-Razi's study, as a picture. The list after it says the same in words.
rzr_objective: Fly along the desk and touch a leaf to lift it, then touch another place to swap the two leaves. When the leaves run from the head down to the foot, touch the binding frame to bind the notebook.
rzr_objective_door: Walk Hudhud to the lit door at the end of the study.
rzr_thing_bundle: the bundle of loose leaves on top of the tall bookcase
rzr_thing_frame: the binding frame at the end of the desk
rzr_places_group: The places on the desk, in order
rzr_razi_hello: Welcome to my study. Ask what you like; the leaves will wait on the desk.
rzr_thanks: Thank you. Now to the desk.
rzr_razi_bye: Go well. The head comes first, and the foot comes last.
rzr_note_room: The room, the desk, the leaves on it and the binding frame are invented for play; they are not a picture of the hospital of Rayy or of where al-Razi worked. There is no medical advice in this game.
